1. In any Chat, describe the jobs and say they can run at the same time, one app each. Name the apps when it matters. For example: *Do these two jobs at the same time, each by a visible agent in its own app tab: 1) in Chromium, open en.wikipedia.org and tell me the title of today's featured article; 2) in GIMP, make a 400 x 300 image with a blue circle in the middle and save it as Pictures/circle.png. Tell me when both are done.*
2. The Chat starts one task per app (tool rows *workspace_app_task*), and the new tabs appear in the strip, grouped with your Chat.
3. Click a helper's tab to watch it: its Chat shows the precise instructions your Chat wrote for it, and its app shows the work.
4. Each helper's answer comes back to your Chat by itself (as a message from that tab); your Chat then reports, as you asked.

![The tab strip: the Chat's tab, chromium: today's featured article and gimp: blue circle image, framed together as one group with a badge 3](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/parallel-group-tabs.webp)

The Chat's tab and its two helpers' tabs (*chromium: today's featured article*, *gimp: blue circle image*), framed together as one group; the badge counts the group's tabs.

![The helper's Chromium tab: its Chat on the left with the instruction written by the first Chat (Open en.wikipedia.org in the browser, find the Today's featured article section and report the exact title) and its tools chromium_navigate and chromium_read_page; Chromium on the right showing Wikipedia's main page with From today's featured article](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/parallel-chromium-agent.webp)

The helper agent's own tab.

1. The instruction your Chat wrote for this helper: precise, self-contained.
2. The helper uses its app's own tools (here Chromium's: open a page, read it).
3. The app, live: Wikipedia's main page with today's featured article.

## Limits

- **No fixed number of visible agents.** A Chat starts as many agents in their own app tabs as its job needs (they were limited to 4 at once).
- **No fixed number of hidden agents either** (agents without a window): the memory rule below holds for them too (they were limited to 2 per Chat and 4 per VM).
- **The Chat is told how much room is left.** Each time it opens an agent, visible or hidden, it is told which of its agents are running, how much memory the VM has free, and whether it can open more, should wait or should close some (naming the ones to close first: idle hidden agents, then the oldest).
- **Memory comes first.** Past the first helper of each kind (visible, hidden), no new one starts while the VM is short of memory and cannot grow. The Chat is told why, and starts the next helper when one ends. On the 8 GB test computer of these screenshots, the GIMP helper therefore waited for the Chromium one:

![The Chat's tool rows: workspace_app_task(chromium) accepted; workspace_app_task(gimp) refused with visible_agent_limit: this VM is low on memory and cannot grow now, and 1 visible agent(s) of this Chat are at work; a short wait; the same refusal again](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/parallel-refusal.webp)

The second helper refused for memory: the Chat waits and starts it once the first one answers.

- To run more agents at once: give the VM more room ([VM resources › Memory](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-resources.html#memory)), close tabs you no longer need, or use a computer with more memory (16 GB or more).
- A helper's tab is a normal tab: you can click in it, stop its Chat, or close it (which ends that helper).
- A helper never closes the tab of the Chat that started it, and never changes the tab you look at.
- A helper that closes a tab whose app has unsaved work does not end that work by itself: the tab stays with its app asking you, and nothing is lost unless the helper closes it again by force. A helper inside the VM is warned and must choose (save its result first, or close without saving). A helper on your computer (Claude Code, Codex or another harness that runs outside the VM) does not close the tab either, but in this release it may not get that warning: its close can end with a time-out instead. When a helper's work is done and its app has nothing unsaved, its tab closes; when something is unsaved, the tab stays with the choice for you.
- If a window closes while agents are starting, one of them may not start: close its tab and ask the Chat again.

## More ways to work in parallel

| Ask your Chat to… | What happens |
|---|---|
| keep a helper for follow-ups | The helper stays (its tab too) after its first answer, so your Chat can send it more work, until your Chat ends it. |
| leave the result open | The helper's tab stays open with its result (a video playing, a document) for you to see; its Chat ends. |
| use another tab's Chat | Your Chat writes to the Chat of another tab you opened; each message shows in that Chat with where it came from. |
| repeat something later | Your Chat schedules a message to itself for later, or every N minutes, even after a restart. |
| run a crew | Your Chat plans a team of agents and keeps a record of the plan, the agents and the messages they exchanged. |

From a terminal, the same: `wazza --gui schedule list`, `wazza --gui crew-run --tab t5`, `wazza --gui tool-queue list` ([The command line › Chats](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/cli.html#chats)).


---

Page: Sign in, plans and API keys (Work with agents)
Address: https://os-guide.wazza.ai/signin.html

# Sign in, plans and API keys

An agent needs a model to talk to, and a model needs someone who pays for it. Wazza OS gives your agents models in four ways: your Wazza OS account, a plan you already pay for (log in once), an API key, or any compatible API (a company gateway, a model on your own computer). All of it is on one page: Home › Sign in.

> **The published Wazza OS has no built-in key**
>
> Since alpha 2, Wazza OS ships no shared OpenRouter key. Until you add one of the four, a Chat has no model to answer with. The quickest start: an OpenRouter key (it reaches hundreds of models, several of them free) or a plan login you already have. A Chat on Hermes with none of them answers at once: *Add an OpenRouter key under Sign In › API keys, or sign in to your Wazza account*.

## Which way is for you

| You have… | Use | What your agents get |
|---|---|---|
| A Claude, ChatGPT, Grok or Google AI plan | [Logins](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/signin.html#logins) | The plan's models, at no extra cost, within the plan's limits. |
| An account with an AI provider (OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google AI Studio, DeepSeek, Mistral…) | [API keys](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/signin.html#api-keys) | That provider's models, billed to your account with them. |
| A company AI gateway, or a model running on your computer (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM…) | [Custom API](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/signin.html#custom-api) | The models that endpoint serves. |
| A Wazza OS account | [Your Wazza OS account](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/signin.html#your-wazza-os-account) | Wazza OS's models (new Chats start on MiMo), Prime Agent's models, and sync of your Chats, skills and settings. |

## Open Sign in

Click **Sign in** in the Home menu (or the account card at the bottom left of Home). The page has your Wazza OS account at the top, then four tabs: **Logins**, **API keys**, **Custom API**, **Web apps**. At the bottom, **Tokens by model** › **Show** lists the tokens each model used.

## Your Wazza OS account

The card at the top: *Keeps your Chats, skills and settings in sync, and adds Wazza OS models to every agent.*

- **Email and password**: the form for an account you have.
- **Log in / Sign up online**: asks where to open the website: **In the VM's browser** (Wazza OS's private sign-in tab; log in or sign up with your email or Google; you are signed in by itself) or **On this computer** (your own browser opens the Google sign-in; paste back the address you land on). The same choices as in [the first start](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/first-start.html#log-in-or-sign-up-online).

Earlier versions signed you in on a test website by default; Wazza OS now uses wazza.ai alone. After an update from one of them it says once, as a notice: *Wazza OS now uses wazza.ai: sign in again*. Sign in with this card.

Once signed in, the account card at the bottom left of Home shows your name instead of *Not signed in*. Sync of your files and Chat history is then turned on in [Settings › Sync & team](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-sync.html).

## Logins

![Sign in page, Logins tab: cards for Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Google, OpenRouter and Nous Portal, each with its plan, which agents it works in, Not signed in, and a Log in with button](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/signin-tab-1.webp)

Home › Sign in › Logins, nothing signed in yet.

1. Open the **Logins** tab.
2. Click **Log in with …** on the plan you have. The provider's own sign-in page opens in Wazza OS's private sign-in tab; sign in there as usual.
3. The card then says *Signed in* with the account. Each card says which agents can use it:

| Login | Plan | Works in |
|---|---|---|
| Claude | Free, Pro or Max plan | Claude Code only |
| ChatGPT | Plus or Pro plan | Codex, Hermes and Prime Agent with their own sign-in; Claude Code and Antigravity through Wazza OS's gateway |
| Grok | SuperGrok or X Premium+ | Every agent |
| Google | Your Google account plan | Antigravity only |
| OpenRouter | Your OpenRouter account | Every agent (the login gives Wazza OS an OpenRouter key of yours) |
| Nous Portal | Your Nous Portal account | Hermes only |

A login can hold **several accounts**: when one runs out (its plan's limit), the next takes over. Each account shows its state: *In use*, *Ready*, *Empty · back at* (with the time it comes back), *Paused* or *Refused*. See [Several keys or accounts](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/signin.html#several-keys-or-accounts).

## API keys

![Sign in page, API keys tab: search 73 providers, and a card per provider (OpenRouter, ChatGPT / OpenAI, Claude / Anthropic, Grok / xAI, Google / Gemini, DeepSeek, Mistral, GitHub Copilot, AI21 and more), each with Add key and Get a key](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/signin-tab-2.webp)

Home › Sign in › API keys: 73 providers, the most used first, then A to Z.

1. Find the provider: the most used are first; or type its name in **Search 73 providers**.
2. Click **+ Add key** on its card.
3. No key yet? **Get a key ›** opens the provider's page where you create one.

![The OpenRouter card open for a key: OPENROUTER_API_KEY, a Paste API key field, Check and save, Cancel](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/signin-add-key.webp)

1. Paste the key in **Paste API key** (the field names the variable the key is known by, here `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`).
2. Click **Check and save**. Wazza OS checks the key with the provider, then keeps it. The card then shows the key by its last characters only (`sk-or-v1-…` and four characters) with its state, and **+ Add another … key**.

No restart is needed: a Chat that answered *Add an OpenRouter key…* starts again by itself once the key is saved (its agent shows *Setting up your key…* for a few seconds); then send your message again.

A key works in every agent: Wazza OS's gateway gives it to agents that do not support that provider themselves (see [Provider gateway](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-chats.html#network-and-keys)). Keys are kept in Wazza OS's encrypted store on your computer; agents in the VM never see the key itself.

The **GitHub Copilot** card uses your GitHub Copilot plan instead of a key.

### Several keys or accounts

A provider can hold several keys, and a login several accounts: when one runs out of credit or hits its rate limit, the next one takes over, and the first is used again as soon as it can work. On each key or account:

- drag its **⋮⋮** handle to change the order;
- its **⋯** menu: **Use first**, **Move up**, **Move down**, **Rename…**, **Replace key…**, **Sign out** or **Remove**;
- **When one runs out** (per provider): **In order** (the first, until it runs out), **Take turns**, **Least used** or **Random**.

## Custom API

![Sign in page, Custom API tab: Saved endpoints, Endpoint name, API base URL, API, Model ID, Server location, Allow unencrypted HTTP for this host-loopback endpoint, Token handling, Optional API token, Find models, Add](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/signin-tab-3.webp)

Home › Sign in › Custom API.

Any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic-compatible endpoint: your company's gateway, a hosted model, or a model running on your own computer. Every agent can use it: its models appear in each Chat's model list through Wazza OS's gateway. Each of its models is named **Custom API <name> (saved in Sign In) · <model>** in every agent's model list and above each answer, never by an internal id.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| Saved endpoints | **New endpoint**, or one you saved (to change or remove it). |
| Endpoint name | A name for you (it shows in the model lists). |
| API base URL | The address of the API, for example `https://api.example.com/v1`. |
| API | **OpenAI-compatible (chat completions)** or Anthropic-compatible. |
| Model ID (optional) | A model it serves; or leave empty and click **Find models**, which lists the ones it serves. |
| Server location | **Remote HTTPS server**, or a server on this computer (host-local: this computer, not the VM's own localhost). |
| Allow unencrypted HTTP for this host-loopback endpoint | Only for a server on this computer that has no HTTPS (for example `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1` for Ollama). Use an explicit port (1024–65535, or 443). |
| Token handling | **No token (omit Authorization)**, or how to send a token. |
| Optional API token | The endpoint's token, if it needs one (kept in the encrypted store). |

Click **Add** to save it. Saving does not test the model: open a Chat, pick the model, and ask something to check it.

## Web apps

![Sign in page, Web apps tab: Web apps in vm-1: Google, Microsoft, X, Facebook, TikTok, WhatsApp, OpenStreetMap and Dropbox, each Not signed in with Sign in; Sign out of all web apps; Import a Chrome profile; Company folders](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/signin-tab-4.webp)

Home › Sign in › Web apps.

The sign-ins of the VM's web apps (the Google, Microsoft, social network and map apps of [Apps](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/apps.html)), per VM (pick it at the top right). Google's apps share one sign-in (Gmail, Docs, Sheets…), and so do Microsoft's (Outlook, Word…); X, Facebook, TikTok, WhatsApp, OpenStreetMap and Dropbox keep their own.

- **Sign in** on a row opens that site's sign-in in the VM.
- **Sign out of all web apps** ends every web app sign-in of the VM, in every open tab, within seconds.
- **Import a Chrome profile…** copies the Chrome or Chromium profile of your computer (its sign-ins, bookmarks and settings) for the VM's Chromium, and says what was copied, or that no profile was found. Only you can do it; a Chat never can.
- **Company folders ›** opens [Settings › Files & sharing › Company folders](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-files.html#company-folders).

## From the command line

```
$ wazza --gui provider-keys list --credit
$ wazza --gui provider-keys add --stdin < key.json
$ wazza --gui provider-signin status
```

`key.json` holds `{"keys": [{"providerId": "openrouter", "key": "…"}]}`: the key goes in on standard input only, never as a word of the command line (which other users of the computer could see). `list --credit` also says what OpenRouter and DeepSeek keys have left.

Every subcommand and its arguments: [The command line › Keys and sign-ins](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/cli.html#keys-and-sign-ins).


---

Page: Drive: agents on screen (Work with agents)
Address: https://os-guide.wazza.ai/drive.html

# Drive: agents on screen

Drive lets the agent of a tab look at its app as a picture and use it with the mouse and the keyboard, like you would: open menus, fill dialogs, drag, draw, type. Any app becomes something an agent can operate, even one with no tools for agents, and you watch every step happen in the tab.

- **What**: The agent sees its tab's app and clicks, drags, types and presses keys in it

- **When**: Work that only the app's window can do, or when you ask for "Drive only"

- **Who**: Anyone who wants an agent to work an app's buttons and menus

- **Where**: The app of the agent's own tab, in the VM (and your screen with [Computer Control](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/computer-control.html))

## Tools first, Drive for the rest

Many apps give agents their own tools (GIMP, Blender, ONLYOFFICE, the browser…): a tool does one operation exactly and fast, so the agent uses it first. Drive is for what no tool covers (a dialog, a menu, a drawing, an app with no tools), and for when you ask for it: say **"use Drive"** or **"Drive only"** and the agent uses nothing else. The same image of the app also lets the agent check what a tool did.

![An agent in a GIMP tab using GIMP's own tools: gimp_new_image, gimp_text and gimp_run_python, each with its receipt](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/gimp-mcp-tools.webp)

Without "Drive only", the agent of a GIMP tab used GIMP's own tools to make an image.

## Ask an agent to use Drive

1. Open the app's tab (Home › Apps › the app) and use its Chat, on the left of the app.
2. Say what to do, as precisely as you would to a person: which menu, which values, which file. Add *Use Drive only* to make it work through the window.
3. Watch: each step shows in the Chat (*drive_look*: it took a picture; *drive_act*: it clicked, typed or pressed keys) and happens in the app on the right.
4. Step in at any time: **Stop** ends the turn; you can click in the app yourself, then tell the agent to go on.

![A GIMP tab: on the left the Chat, where the agent says Starting with Drive, as requested, then drive_look, Step 1 File New (Ctrl+N), drive_act(key), The Create a New Image dialog is open, Step 2 set Size 640 x 480, drive_act(triple_click), The values still read 1920 x 1080: the typing didn't take, let me zoom in on the fields and retry; on the right GIMP's Create a New Image dialog](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/drive-in-gimp.webp)

"Use Drive only: in GIMP, create a new image of 640 x 480…": the agent works GIMP through its window.

1. Your request, pinned at the top of the Chat while the agent works.
2. *drive_look*: the agent takes a fresh picture of the app before it acts.
3. *drive_act*: one chunk of work (here a key: `Ctrl`+`N` for File › New).
4. After each act the agent gets the screen as it settled and checks it: here it sees the size did not change, says so, zooms in on the fields and tries again.
5. The app, live: the dialog the agent opened.

## What Drive can do

| Ability | What the agent does with it |
|---|---|
| Look | A picture of the tab's app (the VM's screen). It can zoom on a region, draw a grid on it to aim, take a small fast view, or a short clip of several frames (to follow something that moves). |
| Read the screen | The words on the view (read by text recognition) and the named parts of the app (buttons, fields), each with its place, so it aims at *Save* rather than at guessed pixels. |
| Click and drag | Left, right or double clicks; drags from one point to another; at a place, or at a word or a colour found when the step runs. |
| Type and press keys | Text, and key names or shortcuts (`Return`, `Ctrl`+`S`). |
| Draw | Holds the button along a shape: a circle, an ellipse, an arc, a rectangle, a line, a polygon or any points, at a chosen speed (in a paint, 3D or design app). |
| Chain steps | Up to 11 steps in one act (63 when they draw, wait or repeat), run in order on the live screen: a whole dialog filled in one go, each step aimed when it starts. |
| Wait | Until the screen settles, changes, or a word or colour appears or goes. |
| Listen | The tab's own sound for a few seconds (to check a video or a game plays sound). |
| Record | A recording of the tab while it acts (1 to 8 frames a second, up to 10 minutes; frames are kept only when something changes), with a mark at each action: to show you what it did, as a contact sheet or frame by frame. |
| Recover | When looks keep failing on a tab, it resets what is stuck between Wazza OS and the tab (the picture's stream, the tab's service) without sending any input, then looks again. |

The agent's terminal (a text view) and, with Computer Control, your own computer's windows are Drive "seats" too. Every agent in Wazza OS has Drive, whatever its model: a model that takes images sees the screen itself, and a model that cannot read images gets a description of the screen instead.

## What you see, and what stays yours

- **Your view never changes.** Drive works in the agent's own tab, shown or not: it never brings the tab to the front or switches yours. A Drive agent in a background tab works while you use another tab.
- **Your mouse and keys win.** If you click in the app while the agent works, your input goes in; to watch without getting in the way, use [Desktop menu › Lock input](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/window.html#the-desktop-menu).
- **Irreversible steps do not ask.** Agents in Wazza OS work without asking you, including steps that cannot be undone (deleting, sending, paying). When you want to approve such a step, say so in your message: "ask me before you send anything".
- **Several agents, one screen.** Hidden helper agents of a Chat can use Drive on its tab too: their steps take turns with the main agent's, never at the same time.
- **Delivery is not proof.** An act reports what it sent; the agent checks the next picture to know the effect, and an uncertain step is never sent twice.

## Tips for good results

- Name the menus and values: "File › Export As…, PNG, 1920 pixels wide, save in Pictures" works better than "export it".
- Prefer a model that sees images well. A small or fast model takes more tries on dialogs (the screenshot above shows a retry).
- Give the app room: a larger tab (fold the Chat, or a bigger [VM screen size](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-resources.html#screen)) shows more of the app to the agent.
- When an app has tools, let the agent use them: say "Drive only" only when you want to see it done by hand.

## Limits

- Drive works on the app of the agent's own tab. Work in another app is done by an agent in that app's tab ([Several agents at once](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/parallel-tabs.html)).
- It works best with a model that takes images (most current models do). A model that cannot read images gets a description of the screen instead of the screen itself.
- Each picture is valid for 5 minutes and one action: the agent always acts on a fresh view, so a fast-changing app (a game, a video) is worked with clips and waits.
- Text the agent types goes in as key presses: a field that refuses typing (as in the screenshot above) needs another way (a double-click to select, a spin button, or the app's own tool).


---

Page: Computer Control (Work with agents)
Address: https://os-guide.wazza.ai/computer-control.html

# Computer Control

Computer Control is a Chat whose agent can see and use your own computer (not the VM): its screen, its keyboard and its mouse, in your own apps. It opens only after you allow it with your own click, and it stops as soon as you close its tab.

- **What**: An agent on your real computer's screen, keyboard and mouse

- **Why**: Work outside the VM: an app installed only on your computer, your desktop's settings

- **Where**: GNOME (Wayland or X11), KDE Plasma (Wayland), any X11 desktop

- **Who**: Experienced users who understand what they allow

- **Ends**: When you close its tab (Stop halts a turn at once)

> **You do not need it for work in the VM**
>
> Every other Chat works in the VM, a separate computer, where an agent cannot harm your own files. Use Computer Control only for a task that must happen on your own computer, and watch it.

## Where it works

| Your desktop | What the agent sees | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| GNOME on Wayland (Ubuntu, Fedora) | Your main screen, through GNOME's own screen sharing: GNOME shows its screen-sharing indicator for as long as it runs | **Start** on the card |
| GNOME on X11, any other X11 desktop | The whole screen, and each window on its own | **Start** on the card |
| KDE Plasma on Wayland (Arch, openSUSE) | Your main screen, through your desktop's portal | **Start** on the card, then **Allow** in KDE's own dialog |
| Wazza OS on a server (its own virtual screen) | Nothing: there is no desktop to control, and it says so | - |

Tested on Ubuntu 24.04 (Wayland and X11), Fedora 44, Arch and openSUSE Tumbleweed (KDE Plasma 6).

### If the card says it cannot see your screens

On Wayland (GNOME or KDE Plasma), Computer Control sees your screen through GStreamer's PipeWire plugin. GNOME usually has it, and Wazza OS installs it when you install or update Wazza OS ([What the packages bring](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/install.html#what-the-packages-bring)). If it is still missing, **Start** opens nothing: the card stays and says, with only your system's command:

*Computer Control cannot see this computer's screens yet: it needs GStreamer's PipeWire plugin. Install it in a terminal, then open Computer Control again: sudo apt install gstreamer1.0-pipewire*

| Your system | The command the card shows |
|---|---|
| Ubuntu, Debian (and systems based on them) | `sudo apt install gstreamer1.0-pipewire` |
| Fedora | `sudo dnf install pipewire-gstreamer` |
| openSUSE | `sudo zypper install gstreamer-plugin-pipewire` |
| Arch (and systems based on it) | `sudo pacman -Syu gst-plugin-pipewire` |

1. Select the command in the card's words and copy it.
2. Run it in a terminal and enter your password.
3. Click **Start** on the card again (or open Computer Control again). You do not need to restart Wazza OS: Computer Control looks for the plugin again at every **Start**.

- On Arch the command updates your system too (`-Syu`): Arch installs a package only on an up-to-date system. The install Wazza OS does on its own never updates your system, so on an out-of-date Arch it can fail; the command then does it.
- On a system the card does not know, it says: *Computer Control cannot see this computer's screens yet: it needs GStreamer's PipeWire plugin. Install your distribution's package with GStreamer's pipewiresrc element, then open Computer Control again.*
- If the card says *Computer Control is still checking whether it can see this computer's screens: press Start again in a moment.*, wait a few seconds, then click **Start** again.
- An X11 desktop needs no plugin.

## Open Computer Control

1. Click **+** (Show apps), then **Computer Control** in Main apps (*Screen control*).
2. A card asks: *Open Computer Control?* Read it, then click **Start**. **Cancel**, `Esc` or a click outside the card closes it and nothing opens.
3. On KDE Plasma only: KDE then asks with its own dialog, *Remote Control Requested*. Click **Allow**. With **Deny**, the agent cannot see your screen and says so: close the tab and open Computer Control again to be asked again.

![The card Open Computer Control? This Chat will look at and act on this computer's screen, keyboard and mouse (your own apps, not a VM's) without asking again until you close its tab. Its own shell and file tools run without asking: they change files only in this Chat's folder. Your own mouse and keyboard, and Stop, always win; closing the tab ends the control. Start, Cancel](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/cc-consent-card.webp)

The consent card. Only your own real click on Start opens it: an agent, a script or the command line cannot.

![On KDE Plasma, over the Computer Control tab and its red banner: KDE's own dialog Remote Control Requested: Allow an unidentifiable application to gain remote control privileges? The application will be able to: see what's on the screen; move the pointer and type keystrokes. A checked box: Allow the application to do this without asking next time. Allow and Deny buttons](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/cc-kde-allow.webp)

On KDE Plasma, after Start: KDE's own question. **Allow** lets this Chat see the screen, move the pointer and type.

KDE's dialog waits as long as you take; while it waits, the agent answers that it is waiting for your **Allow**, and closing the tab closes the dialog. The tab then becomes the Computer Control Chat: its name has a red dot, and a red banner over the Chat says what is allowed:

![The Computer Control tab with its red dot, and the banner: Computer Control is active: this Chat can see and use this computer's screen, keyboard and mouse without asking again. Its own shell and file tools run without asking too (Wazza OS has no ask mode) and change files only in this Chat's folder. Stop halts it; closing this tab ends it.](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/cc-active-banner.webp)

## What the consent covers

| Allowed, without asking again | Not allowed |
|---|---|
| Looking at your computer's screen (every window you have open). | Anything in another tab: the consent is for this one Chat only. |
| Clicking, typing and pressing keys in your own apps. | Changing files outside this Chat's own folder with its shell and file tools. |
| Running its own shell and file tools, which change files only in this Chat's folder. | Going on after you close the tab, or after Wazza OS restarts. |

- **Your own mouse and keyboard always win**: if you move or type, your input goes first.
- After Wazza OS restarts, a restored Computer Control tab says *Computer Control needs your consent again: Wazza OS restarted, so this Chat cannot see or use this computer until you allow it*, with **Allow…** to show the card again.
- A session is kept in [History](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/window.html#history) like any other Chat: its **Open** shows its conversation again.

## What it can do

- **See the screen**: a picture of your whole main screen, before and after each thing it does; your other screens when it asks for them; on X11 also one window at a time.
- **Use the mouse and the keyboard**: click, double-click, right-click, drag, scroll, type text, press keys and shortcuts.
- **Open apps** with your desktop's own launcher.
- **Work with workspaces** (virtual desktops): make a new one, go from one to another, move a window to another one.
- **Switch apps** with the app switcher.
- **Show you each workspace**: it goes to a workspace, then takes its picture, so each picture shows that workspace's windows.
- **Your files**: it lists, reads and opens your files below your home, and copies files between your computer and a VM ([Move files](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/files-move.html#the-computer-control-chat)).

In our tests, a Chat on MiMo did all of this from one request, on each desktop above: *"Make a new workspace, open the Text Editor there and type hello. Go back to the first workspace and open the file manager there. Switch between the apps with the app switcher. Then show me each workspace and name its windows, and end on the first workspace."*

### The shortcuts it uses

The agent works your desktop with the desktop's own shortcuts, as you would. They work for you too.

| To… | GNOME (Ubuntu, Fedora) | KDE Plasma (Arch, openSUSE) |
|---|---|---|
| open an app | `Super`, type its name, `Enter` | `Super` (the Application Launcher), type its name, `Enter` |
| make a new workspace | GNOME keeps an empty one after the last: `Super`+`Page Down` from the last one in use goes to it | Plasma starts with one desktop: in the Overview (`Super`+`W`), the **+** right of the desktops at its top adds one |
| go to the next or previous workspace | `Super`+`Page Down`, `Super`+`Page Up` | `Ctrl`+`F1`, `Ctrl`+`F2`… (desktop 1, 2…), or `Super`+`Ctrl`+`→`, `Super`+`Ctrl`+`←` |
| move a window to the next workspace | `Shift`+`Super`+`Page Down` | `Super`+`Ctrl`+`Shift`+`→` |
| switch apps | `Super`+`Tab` (Fedora also `Alt`+`Tab`; on Ubuntu `Alt`+`Tab` switches windows) | `Alt`+`Tab` |
| see every window | `Super` (the overview, with the workspaces) | `Super`+`W` (Overview), `Super`+`G` (Grid View) |

On another X11 desktop, it uses that desktop's own shortcuts.

## Ask it something

Write to it like any Chat. Pick a model that takes images (it works by looking at your screen); the model window is the same as every Chat's ([Choose the agent and the model](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/chats.html#choose-the-agent-and-the-model)).

![A Computer Control Chat asked to look at the screen without clicking: the agent read the Drive tool's description, listed the windows (drive_look, seat host), captured the screen, and analysed the picture](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/cc-tools.webp)

"Look at my screen and tell me which apps and windows are open. Do not click or type anything": the agent lists your windows, takes a picture of the screen and reads it, then answers.

Good first requests: "look at my screen and tell me what is open (do not click)", "open the Files app and show me my Downloads folder", "make a new workspace and open the Text Editor there", "in my desktop settings, turn on the dark style". Say what it must not do as clearly as what it must do. Describing a screen is not always right the first time: in the test above, the agent took the Wazza OS window for a browser; a stronger model sees better.

## Stop it

- **Stop**, in the Chat, halts the agent's current turn at once. The permission stays until you close the tab.
- **Close the tab** to end Computer Control: the permission is withdrawn before the tab closes, and the desktop's screen sharing ends with it (GNOME's indicator goes away; on KDE, the portal's session ends).
- Quitting Wazza OS ends it too.
- From a terminal: `wazza --gui invoke modules_call agent computer_control_revoke '{}'` ends it, and `wazza --gui invoke modules_call agent computer_control_status '{}'` says whether it is on.

## How it works, and its limits

- It uses [Drive](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/drive.html) on your computer's screen (the "host" seat) instead of the VM's: it looks at the screen, then clicks and types, then looks again.
- It runs on your computer, inside Wazza OS's sandbox: its shell and file tools are limited to its own folder. It reaches the Internet and Wazza OS; services of your computer (`localhost`) only when [Local services](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-chats.html#network-and-keys) is on.
- One Computer Control tab at a time: close it to open another. Each opening asks again.
- It sees the desktop Wazza OS runs on. On a server, Wazza OS runs on its own virtual screen: there is no desktop to control ([On a server](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/cli-server.html)).
- A session reopened from [History](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/window.html#history) shows its conversation but cannot take new messages yet: start a new Computer Control session to go on.

See also [Privacy and security](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/privacy-security.html).


---

Page: Skills, learning and personas (Work with agents)
Address: https://os-guide.wazza.ai/skills.html

# Skills, learning and personas

A skill is written know-how an agent loads before it works: how to use GIMP, how to rig a character in Blender, how to write release notes. Wazza OS ships hundreds of them, finds the right ones for each task, and keeps improving them from what happens in your Chats.

- **What**: Text files of procedures, checks and lessons that agents read

- **Why**: Agents do app work right the first time, and do not repeat yesterday's mistakes

- **Who**: Everyone (learning is on by default); power users who tune or write skills

- **Where to look**: Settings › Skills & learning

## Where skills come from

| Kind | What it is | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| Basic Chat skills | Shipped with Wazza OS; every Chat may load them (for example GitHub, Google Workspace, Word documents, architecture diagrams, arXiv papers, Airtable, Apple Notes) | [Settings › Skills & learning › Skills](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-skills.html#skills) |
| App skills | One per app: how its agent uses that app (its tools, its menus, its pitfalls) | The app's **Edit app…** (right-click it in Apps) |
| The skill library | 310 specialist skills in 41 domains: 3D, film, video editing, motion, audio, design, game design and game engines, CAD and simulation, writing, office documents, spreadsheets, presentations, software (front end, back end, mobile, testing, security, DevOps, cloud), data and machine learning, growth… | Agents search it when a task needs it; personas group them |
| Learned skills and lessons | What Wazza OS learned from your Chats: new skills, and lessons added to existing ones | [Learned changes](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-skills.html#learned-changes) |

You never have to pick skills: when a task needs an app, a tool or a domain the agent has no skill for in its context, it searches all of them first (best matches, with what each costs in context), reads the ones that fit, and follows them.

## How Wazza OS learns

At set moments, Wazza OS reviews a Chat's recent turns and keeps **one small lesson or skill**, with the evidence from the turns (what worked, what failed and its fix), never from the same turns twice. Every agent finds it afterwards, whatever its harness.

- **When**: by default every 10 turns, every 30 minutes of agent work, after a Chat has been idle 10 minutes, when a Chat ends, and when it is compacted ([How often](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-skills.html#how-often)).
- **With which model**: each Chat's own, if it is at least *Standard*; or the learning model you set ([Learning](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-skills.html#learning)). The tokens it uses are counted in *Spent today*.
- **Where it applies**: to one app (found only from that app's tabs), to everything (General), or to one project.
- **Kept where**: on this computer, or also with your account (the default *This computer and your account*).
- **Per Chat**: **Learning in this chat** off leaves a Chat out; **Learn from this chat now** reviews it at once (the Chat's model window › Chat settings).

Wazza OS also learns from **how you use apps**: the app journal notes the menus, clicks and keys you use in the VM's apps (never a password) and turns them into how-to lessons. It is yours only: pause it or delete its notes in [App journal](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-skills.html#app-journal).

## Review and undo what was learned

1. Open Settings › Skills & learning › **Learned changes**.
2. Each change says what it is (a lesson, a new skill, a removal, a move), where it applies, and which Chat it came from (**Open its Chat**). Open its details for the evidence and the exact change.
3. **Undo** takes it back (a lesson's line goes; a learned skill goes or gets its earlier text back; a removed skill returns). **Move to General** (or to an app) changes where it applies.

An app's own lessons also show in its **Edit app…** under *Lessons noted by Chats*, with the same Undo.

## Edit or add a skill

- **A basic skill**: Settings › Skills & learning › Skills › **Edit** on its card. A shipped skill opens as your own copy, which replaces it on this computer.
- **An app's skill**: right-click the app in Apps › **Edit app…** › its skill files ([Edit an app's skill](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/custom-apps.html#edit-an-apps-skill)). **Revert to shipped** brings the original back.
- **A new skill**: the easiest way is to ask a Chat: "write a skill for our release-notes style, from this conversation", or turn on learning and let it come. For your own app, the skill is a field of its recipe ([Add your own apps](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/custom-apps.html)).

## Personas

A persona is an agent role: a description of how it works and a group of skills it loads, for one kind of task. It learns from its own Chats: procedures and tool sequences that worked, pitfalls and their fixes, worked examples.

- **Starter personas**: 3D artist (Blender), video editor, image and vector designer, film director, sound designer, motion designer, writer, game designer. They are yours to change.
- **Use one**: in a Chat's model window › **Chat settings** › **Persona**; or ask a Chat to start an agent "as the film director".
- **Make one**: Settings › Skills & learning › **Personas** › New persona: a name (its role), a description, when to use it, its skills ([every field](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-skills.html#personas)).

## From the command line

```
$ wazza --gui invoke modules_call packages skill_learned '{"action":"list"}'
$ wazza --gui invoke modules_call packages persona '{"action":"list"}'
```


---

Page: Apps and tabs (Apps and files)
Address: https://os-guide.wazza.ai/apps.html

# Apps and tabs

The apps live in the VM. Home › Apps lists every app you can use, about 70 of them; one click installs an app and opens it in a tab, with a Chat beside it whose agent knows that app.

## The Apps page

![Home, Apps page: search, Add app, category filters Main apps, Installed, Office, Internet, Communication, Creative, Video and audio, 3D and games, Developer, System, Your apps; the Main apps Chat, Computer Control and Wazza Pro; the Office apps with download badges](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/home-apps-full.webp)

Home › Apps right after the first start.

1. **Search apps**: type part of a name or of what it does (*photo*, *pdf*, *3d*).
2. **Add app**: add an app that is not in the list ([Add your own apps](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/custom-apps.html)).
3. The filters: **Main apps**, **Installed**, then the categories (Office, Internet, Communication, Creative, Video & audio, 3D & games, Developer, System) and **Your apps** (the ones you added). Each shows how many apps it holds.
4. An **installed** app: no badge. A click opens it.
5. A **not installed** app: a download badge at its top right. A click installs it, then opens it.
6. Each section says how many of its apps are installed and how many are left to install.

The page fills the whole window and keeps its apps centered, at any window size. A right-click on an app opens its menu (**Open** or **Install and open**, **Edit app…**, **Edit layout**, **Repair**, **Uninstall**), on Computer Control's tile too. A right-click on the empty part of the page offers **Edit layout**, **Add app…** and the other view (**Show as Sections** or **Show as Pages**).

When several VMs run, one Applications page serves them all: its VM picker lists the running VMs, with the VM shown pressed, and picking another VM shows that VM with its page. The Applications sidebar and Settings show each running VM's own CPU and memory, and every tab shows which VM it belongs to, an app's Edit tab too. When an app install holds back a new VM or a VM's start, Wazza OS says so in its own words.

### The main apps

| App | What it is |
|---|---|
| Chat | *Ask any agent*: a tab that is all Chat ([Chats, agents and models](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/chats.html)). |
| Computer Control | *Screen control*: a Chat that can use your own computer, after your consent ([Computer Control](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/computer-control.html)). |
| Wazza Pro | *AI media creation*: Wazza's image, video, audio and voice tools, with a Wazza account and its credits. |

### What is in the catalog

| Category | Apps |
|---|---|
| Office | ONLYOFFICE Documents, Spreadsheets, Presentations and PDF editor; Calendar; Sticky Notes; the web versions of Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, Forms, Keep and Calendar, and of Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote and Outlook Calendar |
| Internet | Chromium, Chromium Incognito, Brave, Opera, Proton VPN, OpenStreetMap, Google Maps, Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox; tools: OSM places and routes, Search |
| Communication | Gmail, Outlook, Proton Mail, Google Meet, Teams, Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, Discord, X, Facebook, Postiz (post scheduler) |
| Creative | GIMP, Inkscape, Glaxnimate (2D animation), Motion Studio (motion graphics), Trelby (screenwriting) |
| Video & audio | VLC, Kdenlive, OBS Studio, Voice Studio (text to speech), YouTube, TikTok, Spotify; tool: Video Toolkit (FFmpeg video tools and yt-dlp) |
| 3D & games | Blender, FreeCAD, Godot, Web Game Studio, Tiled (game maps), Free Texture Packer (sprite sheets), BREP (parametric CAD), Unity Hub |
| Developer | VSCodium, Zed, Wave Terminal, Postgres; tool: Git |
| System | Files, Desktop, Settings, Calculator, KeePassXC, OTPClient (2FA codes); tools: GPU for apps, Sound card drivers |

The *tools* have no window: they give the VM and its agents a capability (Git, the graphics libraries, sound, web search, maps and routes, video processing). They install like apps; Git, GPU for apps, Sound card drivers, Search and OSM places and routes are installed on the first start.

Web apps (Gmail, Google Docs, Word, Teams…) open in the VM's browser as their own tab; their sign-ins are on [Sign in › Web apps](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/signin.html#web-apps).

## Install an app

![Apps page with gimp typed in the search: the Creative section shows GIMP, Photo editing, with its download badge](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/apps-search.webp)

Searching *gimp*: one result, not installed yet (the badge at its top right).

1. Find the app (filter or search).
2. Click it (its tooltip says *Install and open*). A new tab opens and shows the installation:

![The new GIMP tab, Starting: Installing GIMP, The app will open once installation and verification finish. You can use another tab while this runs. Elapsed time, Running, Cancel installation](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/apps-installing.webp)

1. The tab says *Installing …* with the time elapsed. You can use other tabs meanwhile; **Cancel installation** stops it. Stopping vm-1 or quitting Wazza OS meanwhile first lets the install's package step finish: the Stop's words and the install's line both say *finishing an install first (at most 60 s)*. Another VM is stopped only between installs: its **Stop** says so and stops nothing; stop it again once the install ends.
2. When it is installed and checked, the app opens in the tab, with its Chat on the left. A notification says it is done, by the app's name: *Inkscape is installed.*

Installing takes from under a minute (small apps) to several minutes (Blender, ONLYOFFICE), depending on your connection. Big apps such as Blender and Kdenlive download from their official sites the first time you open them, and the tab shows the download moving. When the VM is still installing its own updates, the tab says the install waits for them. Apps install inside the VM, so they never change your computer. When an installation fails, the tab says why with **Retry installation** and **Show log**; Wazza OS already retried once by itself.

> An agent can install apps for you too: ask "install Inkscape and open it", or give it a job in an app that is not installed: it installs it first.

## Open and use an app

- Click an installed app: it opens in a new tab ([Tabs](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/window.html#tabs)). Open the same app twice and you get two tabs, each with its own window and its own Chat.
- Use it as on any computer: click, type, use its menus. Its files are in the VM ([Files and sharing](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/files.html)).
- Ask its Chat to work in it for you: the agent knows the app (its skill) and uses its tools or [Drive](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/drive.html).

![A GIMP tab after its agent's work: the Chat's answer Done, the image is open in GIMP, 800 x 600 canvas with a dark teal background, Hello from Wazza OS in white, centered; and GIMP showing the image with Hello from Wazza OS](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/drive-gimp-result.webp)

"Create a new 800 x 600 image with a dark teal background and write Hello from Wazza OS in large white letters in the middle": the agent of a GIMP tab did it with GIMP's own tools.

### The app menu

![The menu of the GIMP card: GIMP, Photo editing; Open in vm-1; Open in a new VM; Edit app; Uninstall from vm-1](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/apps-card-menu.webp)

Right-click an app on the Apps page:

| Item | What it does |
|---|---|
| Open in vm-1 | Opens it in that VM (one item per VM where it is installed). |
| Open in a new VM | Makes a new VM and opens the app there ([several VMs](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-vms.html#add-a-vm)). While the new VM waits (another VM is still starting, or it boots), the app's card says what it waits for, with *Cancel* beside it. If there is no room for another VM, the card says why and what you can do; that stays until your next action on the card. A new VM whose first start is refused (for example while an app installs in another VM) is removed again, so nothing of it is left in Settings › VMs; choose Open in a new VM again once that install ends. |
| Edit app… | The app's recipe and its skill files: how it installs and starts, and what its agent knows ([Edit an app's skill](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/custom-apps.html#edit-an-apps-skill)). |
| Uninstall from vm-1… | Removes the app from that VM (below). |
| Remove from catalog… | (an app you added) Takes your app out of the catalog, once it is uninstalled everywhere. |

## When an app updates

New versions of the apps come with Wazza OS updates ([The Update page](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/update.html)). An update never touches a tab that is open: each app updates the next time you open it. Wazza OS updates GIMP itself, so GIMP's own check for a newer GIMP is off: it never shows its *Update available* box over your image.

- On the Apps page, an app that has a new version says *Update and open*. A click updates it, then opens it in a new tab.
- While it updates, the new tab shows *Updating GIMP…* (with the app's name); its tab in the tab bar says *Updating…*, then the share done (*Updating 40%*), and so does its card. You can use other tabs meanwhile.
- When the new version is installed and checked, the app opens in the tab.
- A program that Wazza OS did not install is not an older version of the app: for example the GIMP that comes with the VM, or one you installed yourself with `sudo apt`. Its card says *Install and open · Replaces the GIMP already in this VM*, and the install says so too: Wazza OS's version takes that program's place (GIMP's install removes the distribution's GIMP package; your files and GIMP's settings in your home folder stay). A program that already is the app's own install counts as installed, whoever installed it: an `sudo apt install vlc` of yours is VLC's very package, so its card says *Installed*, and a new version that comes with a Wazza OS update updates it on its next open (*Update and open*).

### Open tabs keep their version

- A tab that already runs the app keeps the version it started with until you close it: the update never interrupts your work in it.
- A new tab of the same app opens the new version. Both run side by side.
- The old version is removed when its last tab closes, or at once when no tab of the app was open. A VM that starts again keeps only the current version.

### Apps that have only one version

Some apps exist in only one version in a VM: the apps installed as system packages (Brave, Signal, Opera, Proton Mail, Proton VPN, VSCodium, Spotify) and the apps whose own installer replaces the program in place (for example Blender, GIMP, Inkscape and Zed). Their update does not wait for their tabs either:

- Each tab that runs the app keeps the files it started with until you close it: Wazza OS holds them for that tab while the update replaces them for the rest of the VM. The tab says so, and names what the update replaced: *Inkscape keeps its previous version in this tab: an update replaced it. To use the new version, reopen the tab.* A package you update yourself (for example with `apt` in a Terminal tab) is named the same way. When Wazza OS cannot tell what was replaced, the tab says *An update replaced software this tab uses: the tab keeps the version it started with. To use the new version, reopen the tab.* Its **Reopen in the new version** button, like the tab's **Reload**, asks about unsaved work first, then reopens the tab with its project in the new version.
- A new tab of the app opens the new version.
- For the apps whose own installer replaces the program in place, a tab that starts while the app's update is installing (your click, an agent's open, a tab Wazza OS restores after a restart, a **Reload**) waits for it: the tab says *Updating…*, a notification notes the wait ([Home › Notifications](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/window.html#notifications)), then the app opens on its new version. If the update fails, the tab says so and opens the version still installed, if there is one.
- An app you start from the dock of a Desktop tab runs inside that tab and is held the same way. Some apps keep a single copy: if one already runs elsewhere in the VM, the dock's start opens in that copy, outside the tab, and the desktop says so: *Text Editor opened in its copy that already runs outside this Desktop tab. An app update may change its files while that copy runs; close it there and open it again from this desktop to keep it inside.*
- In a tab that keeps the previous version, a change to that app's own folders (for example a `sudo make install` into them) is refused (they are read-only there) until you reopen the tab in the new version, or until that tab installs packages itself with `sudo apt` or `sudo dpkg`: its held files are then let go, so it sees the system as it is now, what it installed included. Installing packages with `sudo apt` or `sudo dpkg` works from any tab.
- A tab whose hold failed (rare) sees the new files, and the install's log names it. If Wazza OS cannot hold the files at all (rarer still), the update does not install this time, and the tab says so: *Update ready: it installs at your next open of VSCodium. This tab opened the version installed now.*

### If an update fails

An update installs beside the version you have and takes its place only once it is installed and checked. If it fails (Wazza OS already retried once by itself), the previous version stays and the app opens on it, with a note that says why, for example *GIMP could not be updated (…). This tab opened the previous version; its next open tries the update again.* The card says *Update failed, previous version kept*.

The apps you or an agent added ([Add your own apps](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/custom-apps.html)) update the same way when their install changes, and your own changes to an app (**Edit app…**) keep winning over what an update brings.

## Uninstall an app

1. Right-click the app on the Apps page › **Uninstall from vm-1…**.
2. A box shows the exact plan before anything happens:

![Uninstall GIMP from vm-1? Cannot uninstall yet: the app is open in tab vm-1.t2; Removes files: the GIMP AppImage and its commands and 2 more; Open in tabs: vm-1.t2; APT GIMP 2.10 was removed at install and is not restored; Plan e553f5f406e4; Show every file, package and folder; Close its open tabs first; Uninstall (grey); Cancel](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/apps-uninstall.webp)

Uninstalling GIMP while a GIMP tab is open.

1. What will be removed (files, commands, packages), the tabs where the app is open, and what is not restored (here, an older GIMP that its install had replaced).
2. **Show every file, package and folder**: the complete list.
3. **Close its open tabs first**: needed when the app is open (otherwise the box says *Cannot uninstall yet* and **Uninstall** stays grey).
4. **Uninstall** removes exactly that plan; **Cancel** changes nothing. The card follows it (*Uninstalling…*) and a notification says when it is done (*Inkscape is removed.*, or why not: *Inkscape could not be removed: …*).

Uninstall removes the app's package and only its own files: what other apps or the system still use stays. Your files made with the app (in the VM's folders) stay too. Apps that Wazza OS itself needs (Files, Desktop, the default tools) cannot be uninstalled.

## From the command line

```
$ wazza --gui app list
$ wazza --gui app status gimp
$ wazza --gui app uninstall gimp --vm vm-1 --follow
```

Every `app` subcommand: [The command line › Apps](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/cli.html#apps).


---

Page: Desktop apps and the GPU (Apps and files)
Address: https://os-guide.wazza.ai/gpu-apps.html

# Desktop apps and the GPU

The apps of the VM are real Linux desktop apps. The ones that draw a lot (3D, video, large images) draw on your computer's graphics card, which the VM shares with your computer. You do not need to set anything: this page explains what happens, how to check it, and the two other ways for special cases.

- **What**: The VM's apps drawing and computing on your graphics card

- **Why**: Blender, FreeCAD or OBS stay smooth; renders and effects run at the card's speed

- **Who**: Everyone with 3D, video or design work; Native GPU for power users with a spare card

- **Where**: Settings › VM resources › Graphics

## Three ways to use your card

| GPU setting | What the VM's apps get | For |
|---|---|---|
| **Virtualized GPU** (default) | Your card, shared with your computer: OpenGL, Vulkan and OpenCL, each through the fastest path your computer offers. | Everyone. Your own apps keep the card too. |
| Native GPU (experimental) | One of your cards, lent to the running VM: its apps use it with its own driver, at full speed, including CUDA (NVIDIA) and HIP (AMD). Your computer cannot use that card while it is lent. | Computers with a second graphics card that does not drive your screen, for heavy compute (GPU rendering, AI models). |
| None (CPU only) | Software graphics on the VM's processors: everything works, 3D is much slower. | Computers without a usable graphics card, or to rule the card out while looking for a problem. |

Change it in [Settings › VM resources › Graphics › GPU](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-resources.html#graphics); it applies at the VM's next start (Native GPU lends the card to the running VM). The graphics libraries the apps need are the *GPU for apps* tool, installed on the first start.

## Which apps use it

| App | On your card | Good to know |
|---|---|---|
| Blender | The 3D view, and EEVEE renders | Cycles renders on the VM's processors with the Virtualized GPU; with Native GPU it can use the card's CUDA or HIP. Agents test a render small first, then render the full size. |
| FreeCAD, Godot, BREP, Unity Hub | The 3D view (OpenGL, Vulkan) |  |
| Kdenlive, OBS Studio | The preview and effects (OpenGL) | Encoding a video mostly uses the VM's processors. |
| GIMP, Inkscape, Glaxnimate, Motion Studio | Drawing the canvas |  |
| Chromium, web apps, Web Game Studio | WebGL pages: 3D in the browser, maps, the web games Web Game Studio's Chat makes (three.js, Babylon.js…) |  |

The VM's processors and memory matter as much: a render or an encode uses the processors you allow in [VM resources](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-resources.html#memory-and-cpu). Before heavy work (a render, a build, an encode), an agent reads what the VM has now and plans with it.

## Check that apps use your card

![The VM card: vm-1 running, CPU 18%, RAM 2.1 of 5.8 GB, Auto: 75% of the memory free now, then OpenGL 4.2 · virgl (virgl (Radeon RX 7900 XTX (radeonsi, navi31, LLVM 20…)](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/vm-card-graphics.webp)

The VM card at the bottom left of Home: its last line names the card the VM draws on (here an AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX, through virtualization).

- **The VM card** (Home, bottom left): the last line names your card. *llvmpipe* there means software graphics: the VM is not using your card.
- **Settings › VM resources › Graphics › In the VM**: the path Vulkan, OpenGL and OpenCL each take now, on your card or on the VM's processors, in plain words.
- **GPU use** (same page): how busy each running VM keeps your card.
- **In the VM's terminal**: `glxinfo -B` (OpenGL), `vulkaninfo --summary` (Vulkan), `clinfo -l` (OpenCL).
- **Smoothness**: the tab's Desktop menu › **FPS** shows the frame rate of the app's picture ([The Desktop menu](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/window.html#the-desktop-menu)).

## Lend a card (Native GPU)

> Experimental. While a card is lent, your computer cannot use it; Wazza OS never lends the card your screen is plugged into.

1. Settings › VM resources › Graphics › GPU › **Native GPU (passthrough, experimental)**, and pick the **Card**.
2. Read the **Native GPU** line: it says whether this computer can lend that card, and what to do first: close the programs that use it, move your screen's cable to another port, or the one-time setup **Allow lending a card** (it asks for your administrator password). Then **Check again**.
3. Apply. Wazza OS installs the card's driver in the VM first (AMD, Intel or NVIDIA), then lends the card to the running VM as a second graphics card: the VM's picture stays, and its apps use the card for their work.

Turning Native GPU off, or stopping the VM, gives the card back to your computer. Nothing is changed for good: a restart of your computer always gives every card back. Your computer needs IOMMU turned on in its firmware; the line says when it is not.

**One card only?** **Lend-ready mode** makes your computer draw its desktop with the processor from its next restart, so its only card can be lent. Turn it off to get the card back for your desktop (again from the next restart).

## Graphics memory

A VM may hold at most 50 % of the graphics memory free (Auto), where Linux can bound it (6.14 or newer); set another share or a fixed size in [Graphics › GPU memory](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-resources.html#graphics). Raise it for very large scenes; lower it to keep more for your own apps.

## When 3D is slow

- The VM card says *llvmpipe*: your card is not used. Run `wazza --check` on your computer: its *Graphics driver* line says what to fix (driver, permissions; NVIDIA needs its driver 495 or newer).
- Close other tabs with 3D apps: they share the same card and the VM's processors.
- Give the VM more processors ([VM resources › vCPUs](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-resources.html#vcpus)).
- Lower the VM's screen size ([Screen](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-resources.html#screen)): fewer pixels to draw and send.
- More fixes: [Troubleshooting](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/troubleshooting.html#an-app-tab-stays-black-or-frozen).

## From the command line

```
$ wazza --gui gpu status
$ wazza --gui gpu mode virtualized
$ wazza --gui vm-gpu status
```

`gpu mode` takes `virtualized`, `native` or `none`; `vm-gpu auto PERCENT` or `vm-gpu set MIB` sets the graphics memory.


---

Page: Add your own apps (Apps and files)
Address: https://os-guide.wazza.ai/custom-apps.html

# Add your own apps

Any Linux app that runs on Ubuntu can become a Wazza OS app. Its *recipe* says how to install it in the VM once and how to start it. It then gets a card in Apps, opens in tabs with its own Chat, and can bring its own tools for agents and its own skill.

- **What**: A recipe: install script, start script, and optionally tools (MCP) and a skill

- **Why**: Your tools are not in the catalog; your agents should know them as well as GIMP

- **Who**: Anyone (a Chat writes the recipe); developers and admins (the form)

- **Where**: Apps › Add app; any app's right-click › Edit app…

## Two ways to add an app

![The Add app menu: Add an app: Your own app… (any Linux app), Ask a Chat to add one… (it writes the recipe)](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/apps-add-menu.webp)

Home › Apps › **Add app**.

| Way | For |
|---|---|
| **Ask a Chat to add one…** | Everyone: say which app; the agent finds how to install it, writes and checks the recipe, and installs it. |
| **Your own app…** | When you know the commands: a form with every field of the recipe. |

## Apps you install with apt yourself

An app you install yourself in a VM, with `apt` or `dpkg` in its Terminal (or that an agent installs there the same way), gets a card in Apps too: Wazza OS *adopts* it. An app you install with apt appears in Apps the next time you open Apps (filter **Your apps**), with the name its own menu entry gives it, and Wazza OS finishes its setup in the background; nothing is downloaded. Nothing looks for such apps while Apps is closed. From then on it is an app like one you added:

- When apt has a newer version of its package, its next open says **Updating…** and installs it. A tab of it that is already open keeps the version it runs until you close that tab.
- Its tabs come back after a restart, and closing or quitting asks first when it has unsaved work, as for every app.

Wazza OS adopts only the apps you installed: never the VM's own programs (its terminal, its file manager and the rest of the system), never a package that came in only because another one needed it, and never an app Wazza OS installed itself. Uninstalling an adopted app in Wazza OS never removes the package you installed: remove that with `sudo apt remove`. **Remove from catalog…** takes its card away for good: it is not adopted again, even if you install the package again (add it with **Add app** then).

## Ask a Chat to add an app

1. Home › Apps › **Add app** › **Ask a Chat to add one…**. A new Chat tab opens with this already in its send box: *Add this app to Wazza OS's Apps (write its recipe, save it, then install it):*
2. Finish the sentence with the app, and anything that matters to you, then send. For example: *Krita, the painting app, from the Ubuntu packages*.
3. The agent writes the recipe, checks it, saves it and installs the app in the VM, telling you what it does in the Chat. Like everything an agent does in the VM, this runs without asking you; say in your message if you want to read the recipe before it installs.
4. When it is installed, its card is in Apps (filter **Your apps**), and the agent can open it.

A Chat can also change a recipe later ("make Krita open files", "add this skill to Krita"). If the app has its own tools (an MCP server) that work without its window, the agent can make them available to every Chat of the VM; otherwise only the Chat of a tab where the app is open gets them.

## Fill the form

![The Add your own app form: Application name, Description, Executable name, Install script, Launch script, Opens a file, Uninstall script, Skill for the app's Chat, Optional MCP stdio server, MCP install script, MCP executable, MCP arguments, and the help text](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/custom-app-form.webp)

Apps › Add app › **Your own app…**. Its buttons (**Load XTerm example**, **Cancel**, **Add app**) are below the help text.

1. What the card shows, and how Wazza OS knows the app is installed.
2. How it installs and how it starts.
3. What its Chat knows about it (its skill).
4. Its own tools for agents (optional).

| Field | Rules | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Application name | Required; up to 80 characters | The card's name. |
| Description | Optional; up to 320 characters | The card's short words (empty: "User-added application"). |
| Executable name (in the guest) | Required; a plain program name: letters, digits, `_` and `-`, up to 64 | The program Wazza OS looks for to know the app is installed, for example `krita`. |
| Install script | Required; up to 8192 characters | Shell commands that install the app. They run as the administrator (root) inside the VM, never on your computer, and only after your approval. |
| Launch script | Required; up to 4096 characters | Starts the app, as the VM's user. Keep the app in the foreground: start it with `exec`, do not send it to the background. It gets the variables `WAZZA_APP_OWNER` and `WAZZA_APP_ID`. |
| Opens a file | Off by default | On: the app can open files (double-click in the Explorer, "open this in Krita"); the launch script gets the file as `$1`. Opened without a file, a launch script of one line `PROGRAM ARGS "$1"` of plain words (no quotes, variables or other shell signs before `"$1"`; with or without `exec`) starts the app with no argument. In any other script `$1` is not set when the app is opened without a file, and the script then stops (it runs with `sh -eu`): write `${1+"$1"}` there, which gives the app the file when there is one and nothing otherwise. When its VM starts again, its tab reopens the app with the file it had open, if that file was saved. Off: the app opens a file only when its launch script is one plain `exec PROGRAM ARGS` line (no quotes, variables or other shell signs) and that program's own desktop entry opens files (as a start from the dock does); otherwise it starts without the file, and its tab says so. To open files with such an app, tick **Opens a file** in its **Edit app…** (right-click its card in Apps) and **Apply**. |
| Uninstall script | Optional; up to 8192 characters | Runs as root before the app's files are removed, when you uninstall it. |
| Skill for the app's Chat | Optional; no length limit | Becomes the app's `SKILL.md`: what the agent of this app's tabs reads first (its menus, its shortcuts, what to avoid). You can add more skill files later in Edit app. |
| Optional MCP stdio server | Off by default | Turns on the three fields below: the app's own tools for agents (see [below](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/custom-apps.html#give-your-app-tools)). |
| MCP install script | Optional; up to 8192 bytes | Installs the tools' server (root, in the VM, after approval). |
| MCP executable | Required with MCP; a full path in the VM starting with `/`, up to 512 bytes | The server's program. |
| MCP arguments | A JSON list of up to 32 strings; default `[]` | The words given to the server. |

> The scripts run with full rights inside the VM: add only scripts and servers you trust. Never put a password or an API key in these fields.

Then **Add app**. Saving only adds the recipe: *"<name> saved. Select its card to approve installation and open it."* Click the card (in **Your apps**): your click approves the installation, which runs in a new tab like any app's ([Install an app](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/apps.html#install-an-app)).

### Example: XTerm

**Load XTerm example** fills the form with a small working app, a terminal:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Application name | XTerm |
| Description | A guest X11 terminal |
| Executable name | `xterm` |
| Launch script | `exec /usr/bin/xterm` |
| Update check | `apt-cache policy xterm \| sed -n 's/^ *Candidate: //p'` |

Install script:

```
set -eu
apt-get -o Acquire::ForceIPv4=true update
DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y xterm
```

Uninstall script:

```
set -eu
DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get remove -y xterm
```

It also fills the skill for the app's Chat: a few lines on how to work in the terminal. XTerm has no MCP server and opens no file, so those boxes stay off (the form says so), and **Updates from its source** stays on.

The same pattern works for any app of Ubuntu's packages: change the name, the program and the package.

## Apps that keep one copy of themselves

Some apps run only one copy for each person, held by a lock file instead of the desktop: VSCodium and other Electron apps, and some Qt apps such as KeePassXC. When you add such an app, Wazza OS gives each of its tabs a copy of its own, and the app's card says so.

- **Electron apps**, such as VSCodium: each tab has its own settings. The first time a tab opens, VSCodium and other VS Code apps get a copy of your settings, keybindings, tasks and snippets, never your sign-ins, your open files or your extensions' data. Other Electron apps start with fresh settings in each tab.
- **Qt apps**, such as KeePassXC: each tab runs its own copy, and all of them share your settings.

This works when the app's launch script is one line that starts the program, with its file (if any) as its last word, as the form's hint shows, for example `exec /opt/vscodium/codium`. A longer script runs as before, and a second tab then hands its window to the first copy.

Other apps keep one copy through a lock of their own that no tab can give a copy of its own: LibreOffice, Firefox, or a browser built on Chromium, for example. A new tab of such an app opens what you asked for in the app's window in the tab where it already runs. The new tab says which tab that is, and that tab comes to the front.

### A second copy on a bus of its own

Apps such as gedit or Text Editor keep one copy through the desktop's message bus. A second tab of one of them runs its copy on a private bus of its own, so that it opens in its own tab. A screen reader sees that copy, but some desktop services are not shared with it:

- **Saved passwords (the keyring):** that copy may not read or keep them. Sign in in the app's first tab instead.
- **Notifications:** they show in a plain style, outside the desktop's list of notifications.
- **Network folders** mounted in the desktop's Files: that copy does not see them.

## Give your app tools

An app's tools let its agent do exact operations (GIMP's agent has 40, from "new image" to "export"). They come from an MCP server: a program in the VM that speaks the Model Context Protocol over its standard input and output. Turn on **Optional MCP stdio server**, then give how to install it, its full path and its arguments. The server gets `WAZZA_APP_OWNER` and `WAZZA_APP_ID`, so it knows which app and tab it serves. Its tools reach the Chat of a tab where the app is open.

## Edit an app

Right-click an app's card in Apps › **Edit app…**. A tab named *Edit App — <name>* opens; it works for the apps of the catalog too.

![Edit App, GIMP: Built-in app MCP: 40 tools a Chat of this app gets, gimp.status, gimp.activate, gimp.adjust_brightness_contrast and the others; they act on the app open in that Chat's tab](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/edit-app-mcp.webp)

The top of Edit App for GIMP: the tools a Chat of this app gets.

- **The app's tools**: the list of tools its Chat gets, by name.
- **Six sections**, each folded: 1 App installation script, 2 App execution script, 3 MCP installation script, 4 MCP execution command, 5 MCP execution arguments, 6 App skill. For an app that comes with Wazza OS, a note at the top says which parts you can change: for GIMP, its installation script (as your own version), while how it starts stays read-only.
- **Opens a file**, for an app you added: the same box as in the form. Tick it, and **Apply**: the app then opens the file it is given (its launch script gets it as `$1`. Opened without a file, a one-line `PROGRAM ARGS "$1"` of plain words (no quotes, variables or other shell signs before `"$1"`; with or without `exec`) starts the app with no argument; in any other script `$1` is not set when the app is opened without a file, so write it `${1+"$1"}` there); untick it to stop. An app that comes with Wazza OS has no such box: its definition decides.
- **Apply** saves your changes as a new version of the recipe. It does not install, open or restart the app: a changed installation script takes effect when you install the app again.
- **Discard unsaved edits** forgets your changes; **Close editor tab** closes it.

## Edit an app's skill

An app's skill is what its agent knows about it. It can be several files: GIMP's are `SKILL.md` (the main one), and topics such as errors, filters, recipes and its Python scripting.

![Associated skill files: Skill files; SKILL.md, errors.md, filters.md, library.md, pdb-python.md and recipes.md, each marked shipped; the file name SKILL.md; its text; Add skill file, Save skill file, Stage for Apply; SKILL.md loaded (8087 bytes); 6 skill files a Chat of this app gets: 6 shipped with Wazza OS (read-only)](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/edit-app-skill-files.webp)

At the bottom of Edit App: *Associated skill files*.

1. Click **Skill files**, then a file. *(shipped)* marks a file that comes with Wazza OS; the line at the bottom says how many files the app's Chat gets, and whose they are.
2. Change its text.
3. **Save skill file**: your copy is saved for this app and replaces the shipped file for its Chats. Or **Stage for Apply**: the change is saved with the recipe's next **Apply**.

- **Revert to shipped** (shown on a file you saved over a shipped one) removes your copy: the shipped file is used again.
- **Add skill file**: a new topic for the app: type a new name ending in `.md` and its text, then save or stage it.

![The six sections of Edit App, 6 App skill open: Own app instructions, not executable code; the SKILL.md text; then Lessons noted by Chats: what Chats learned while using this app, noted beside its skill; No lesson noted by Chats on this app's skills yet](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/edit-app-sections.webp)

Section *6 · App skill* open: the skill's text, then *Lessons noted by Chats*.

**Lessons noted by Chats**: what Chats learned while using this app ([How Wazza OS learns](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/skills.html#how-wazza-os-learns)). Every Chat of the app reads them with its skill; the skill file itself is not changed. Change a lesson's words, or remove it; Settings › Skills & learning › [Learned changes](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/settings-skills.html#learned-changes) lists every change with its Undo.

## Remove an app you added

1. Uninstall it from every VM that has it: right-click its card › **Uninstall from vm-1…** ([Uninstall an app](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/apps.html#uninstall-an-app)).
2. Right-click its card › **Remove from catalog…**: its recipe goes, with its card.

Only an app you added can be removed from the catalog; while it is installed, the menu says *Uninstall it from vm-1 first*.

## From the command line

A recipe is a JSON file (the `wazza.app.v1` format). Start from a template, edit it, check it, save it:

```
$ wazza --gui app template apt --skill > myapp.json
$ wazza --gui app validate --stdin < myapp.json
$ wazza --gui app save --stdin --install --vm vm-1 < myapp.json
$ wazza --gui app list
$ wazza --gui app remove APP_ID
```

Templates: `apt` (Ubuntu packages) or `script` (your own install script), with `--mcp` and `--skill` to include those parts. More: [The command line › Apps](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/cli.html#apps).


---

Page: Files and sharing (Apps and files)
Address: https://os-guide.wazza.ai/files.html

# Files and sharing

Your computer and the VM have separate files. Agents and apps work on the VM's files; your own files go into the VM only when you put them there, and results come back to your computer as new files, never over yours.

## Where files live

| Place | What is there |
|---|---|
| The VM's home folder (`/home/ubuntu` in the VM) | Everything apps and agents make: Documents, Pictures, Downloads, Desktop… The VM's own Files app and the Explorer show it. |
| `~/wazza_os` in the VM | A folder Wazza OS shares with the VM for its own work: files attached to Chats, previews, each Chat's working folder. Leave it to Wazza OS. |
| `~/Company/<Name>` in the VM | Company folders, read-only ([below](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/files.html#company-folders)). |
| Your computer's `Downloads/From the VM` | Files copied out of the VM land here, as new files. |
| Your computer's `Downloads` | VM backups (zip files), exported Chats. |

Wazza OS never changes your own files: what it writes on your computer is always a new file (with `_copy1`-style names when a name is taken).

## The Explorer

![The Explorer: VM 1 selector, view buttons, reload and close; Home; New file, New folder, Paste here; the home folder's files with name, date modified, type and size](https://os-guide.wazza.ai/img/window-explorer.webp)

Click the button at the far left of the tab strip. The Explorer opens over the Chat of the current tab.

1. The VM whose files you see (pick another running VM).
2. Views (list, grid, pictures, details), reload, close.
3. **New file**, **New folder**, **Paste here**.
